What Are Some Common Injuries from Accidents?

The severity of an injury does not always match what a scene looks like immediately after a crash. Some of the most serious conditions take hours or days to fully appear, which is why medical evaluation should follow any significant accident, regardless of how a person feels at the scene. Knowing what to look for makes a meaningful difference in how a claim develops.
Common injuries seen in personal injury cases include:
Traumatic Brain Injuries (TBI)
According to the
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
, traumatic brain injuries can range from a mild concussion to permanent damage that affects memory, thinking, movement, and daily life.
Spinal Cord Injuries

Few injuries carry consequences as far-reaching as spinal cord damage. Partial or complete loss of movement and sensation can affect every aspect of a person’s life, from independence to long-term earning capacity.
Broken Bones and Fractures:
Fractures to the wrist, hip, ribs, and vertebrae are common in high-impact collisions. Many require surgical repair and months of rehabilitation before a person can return to normal activity.
Soft Tissue Injuries:
Whiplash, torn ligaments, and muscle damage are frequently dismissed as minor by insurance companies, yet they can cause chronic pain and long-term limitations.
Internal Injuries:
Not all serious injuries are visible. Blunt force trauma can cause internal bleeding and organ damage that may not be immediately apparent but can become life-threatening without prompt medical care.
Burn Injuries:
Fires, chemical exposure, and friction burns often result in permanent scarring and can require years of reconstructive treatment and ongoing medical support.

Every injury listed above can affect the value of a personal injury claim. Medical records, treatment history, and expert opinions often play a major role in determining compensation. For that reason, documenting injuries from the beginning is critical. Once injuries are identified, the next step is determining who is legally responsible.
What Should You Do After a Personal Injury Accident in Fort Collins?
The steps taken immediately after an accident can make a significant difference in the outcome of a claim. If your situation allows, consider taking the following steps:

Seek medical attention right away, even if you feel fine. Some injuries do not show symptoms immediately, and a medical record created on the day of the accident ties your injuries directly to the event.
Call law enforcement so an official report is created. Request a copy as soon as it becomes available.
Document the scene by photographing vehicle positions, property damage, road conditions, and any visible injuries before anything is moved or cleaned up.
Collect names and contact information from anyone who witnessed the accident.
Avoid giving recorded statements to insurance adjusters before speaking with an attorney, as doing so can negatively affect your claim.
Contact a
Fort Collins personal injury lawyer
as soon as possible. Evidence degrades quickly, and legal deadlines begin running from the date of the accident.

Not every situation unfolds the same way, and some of these steps may not be possible depending on the severity of the injuries involved. What matters most is getting medical care first and seeking legal guidance before making any decisions about your claim.
Who Can Be Held At Fault in a Personal Injury Accident?
Fault in a
personal injury case
is rarely limited to one person. Depending on the circumstances of the accident, potentially liable parties may include:
Drivers who cause crashes through distracted driving, speeding, impairment, or failure to yield
Employers and trucking companies when an employee causes an accident while on the job
Property owners and business operators who fail to address dangerous conditions on their premises
Manufacturers of defective products that cause harm, regardless of where in the distribution chain the failure occurred
Government agencies responsible for poorly designed roads, missing signage, or neglected public infrastructure
Identifying every liable party matters because it directly affects the compensation available in a claim. Colorado follows a modified comparative negligence framework under
, which means an injured person can still recover as long as they are less than 50 percent at fault. Insurance companies use this rule aggressively to reduce what they pay. Having a
Fort Collins personal injury lawyer
involved early in the process helps preserve key evidence and ensures fault is assigned accurately.
What Damages Can Be Recovered in a Personal Injury Claim?
In a Fort Collins personal injury claim, compensation falls into three main categories. The
Colorado Jury Instructions
outline how each type of damage is defined and applied in personal injury cases.
Economic damages cover the financial losses directly tied to your injury:
Medical expenses, including emergency care, surgery, rehabilitation, and future treatment
Wages lost during recovery, whether from salaried, hourly, or self-employment work
Reduced earning capacity if the injury affects your ability to work long-term
Property damage, including the repair or replacement of your vehicle
Non-economic damages address the personal toll an injury takes beyond the financial:
Pain and suffering limiting your ability to move through daily life
Emotional distress from the trauma of the accident and the recovery process
Inconvenience caused by the disruption to your routine, responsibilities, and relationships
Loss of enjoyment of life when an injury prevents participation in meaningful activities
These damages were previously limited under Colorado law, but
expanded those limits, allowing injured people to recover more for these losses, with future adjustments tied to inflation.

Punitive damages are not about compensation. They apply when a defendant’s conduct was willful, wanton, or malicious, going beyond ordinary negligence. Their purpose is to hold that party accountable and deter similar behavior in the future. Not every case qualifies, but when the facts support them, they can significantly increase the total recovery.
At

Is There a Time Limit for Filing a Personal Injury Claim?
The
deadline to file a personal injury claim in Colorado
depends on the type of case. Motor vehicle accident claims, including car, truck, and motorcycle accidents, must be filed within three years under
. Most other personal injury cases, such as dog bites, slip and fall, and premises liability claims, carry a two-year deadline under
. Missing either deadline typically results in losing the right to recover compensation, regardless of the circumstances.
There are limited exceptions that can shift that deadline:
Minors may have until their 18th birthday before the two-year period begins
Claims against a government entity require formal written notice within 182 days of the incident
Wrongful death claims carry a separate two-year deadline under
The discovery rule may delay the deadline when an injury was not immediately apparent

While these exceptions exist, they are not the rule. Two years can pass quickly, and evidence does not wait. Surveillance footage gets overwritten, witnesses become harder to reach, and important details fade over time. Consulting with a
Fort Collins personal injury lawyer
as soon as possible allows for a thorough investigation while key evidence is still available.

faqs.question: How much is my personal injury case worth?

children.text: Every case is different, and no attorney can guarantee a specific outcome. The value of your claim depends on the severity of your injuries, the cost of your medical treatment, how the accident has affected your ability to work, and the strength of the evidence against the at-fault party. Cases involving serious or long-term injuries are generally worth more than those involving minor harm that resolves quickly.

faqs.question: Do I have to go to court?

children.text: Not necessarily. Many personal injury claims are resolved through a negotiated settlement before a lawsuit is ever filed. However, if the insurance company refuses to offer fair compensation, filing a lawsuit and taking the case to trial may be the right path. Having a
Fort Collins personal injury lawyer
prepared to litigate gives you leverage that unrepresented claimants rarely have.

faqs.question: What if I was partially at fault for the accident?

children.text: You may still be able to recover compensation. Under Colorado’s modified comparative negligence rule, you can pursue a claim as long as your share of fault is below 50 percent. Your total recovery will be reduced by the percentage of fault assigned to you, but it is not eliminated. Insurance companies often exaggerate a claimant’s share of responsibility to reduce what they pay, which is why having an attorney review the facts matters.

faqs.question: How long does a personal injury case take?

children.text: It depends on the complexity of the case and whether it settles or goes to trial. Straightforward claims with clear liability and documented injuries can be resolved in a few months. Cases involving disputed fault, serious injuries, or multiple parties can take a year or longer. Rushing toward a settlement before your injuries have stabilized almost always costs you money in the long run.
